question: When I write `test("parses input") { ... }` inside a FunSuite, where is that test recorded, and what path does its body take until the runner actually evaluates it, including where the per-test timeout is enforced?
reference: `BaseFunSuite.test` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/FunSuite.scala) builds a `Test` whose body wraps `munitValueTransform(body)` in `waitForCompletion`, i.e. `PlatformCompat.waitAtMost` with `munitTimeout`, passes it through `munitTestTransform` and appends it to `munitTestsBuffer`; `munitTests()` applies the suite transforms, and `MUnitRunner` (`runAsync` -> `runTest` -> `runTestBody`) runs the beforeEach fixtures, calls `test.body()` and then the afterEach fixtures.

question: When `assertEquals` fails on two case-class values, how is the failure message with the line-by-line comparison of the two values produced, and which exception carries it to the runner?
reference: `Assertions.assertEquals` delegates to `Compare.failEqualsComparison` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/Compare.scala), which pretty-prints both values and calls `Diffs.assertNoDiff` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/Diffs.scala); that builds a munit-diff `Diff`, whose `createUnifiedDiff` runs `DiffUtils.diff` (a `MyersDiff`) and `generateUnifiedDiff`; on a difference the handler calls `Assertions.failComparison`, which throws a `ComparisonFailException` (an `org.junit.ComparisonFailure`).

question: On the JVM, how does sbt's request to run a test class end up executing it with munit's own runner instead of a stock JUnit runner, and how do the per-test results get back to sbt?
reference: `munit.Framework` (munit/jvm/src/main/scala/munit/Framework.scala) extends the Java `JUnitFramework` in junit-interface and registers a `CustomFingerprint` mapping `munit.Suite` to `munit.MUnitRunner`; `JUnitRunner.tasks` creates a `JUnitComputer` and a `JUnitTask` per class; `JUnitTask.execute` runs `Request.classes(computer, cls)` on a `JUnitCore`, where `JUnitComputer.getRunner` instantiates `MUnitRunner`, configures it and wraps it in `JUnitRunnerWrapper`; the `EventDispatcher` listener turns JUnit notifications into sbt events through `handler.handle`.

question: When an `assert(...)` fails and its condition wraps a sub-expression in `clue(...)`, how do the source text and runtime value of that sub-expression end up in the failure message?
reference: `clue` takes a `Clue[T]`, built by the implicit macro conversion `Clue.generate` (`ClueMacro`) whose implementation `clueImpl` (munit/shared/src/main/scala-3/munit/internal/MacroCompat.scala, or `MacroCompatScala2.clueImpl` on Scala 2) captures the expression's source text and type; `clue` records it in a buffer that `munitCaptureClues` (Assertions.scala) collects while `assert` evaluates the condition, and `fail` hands the resulting `Clues` to `Lines.formatLine`, which appends them pretty-printed by `Printers.print` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/internal/console/Printers.scala).

question: FunSuite lets a suite customise behaviour at three levels: each individual test, the whole list of tests, and the value a test body returns. How is that mechanism organised, which built-in hooks exist at each level, and what ties the levels together?
reference: Three traits mixed into `BaseFunSuite` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/FunSuite.scala): `TestTransforms` (TestTransform: Test => Test; built-ins munitFailTransform and munitFlakyTransform, applied by munitTestTransform when a test is registered), `SuiteTransforms` (SuiteTransform: List[Test] => List[Test]; munitIgnoreSuiteTransform and munitOnlySuiteTransform, applied by munitSuiteTransform in munitTests()) and `ValueTransforms` (ValueTransform: a partial function from a body's value to a Future; munitFutureTransform, applied by munitValueTransform).

question: How are fixtures organised in munit: which types exist for resources shared by a whole suite versus set up around a single test, and how does the runner order the suite's own beforeAll/beforeEach/afterEach/afterAll methods relative to the registered fixtures?
reference: `AnyFixture` (with the `Fixture` and `FutureFixture` subclasses) has beforeAll/beforeEach/afterEach/afterAll and is registered through `Suite.munitFixtures`; `FunFixture` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/FunFixtures.scala) wraps setup/teardown around one test via `FunFixture.test`. `MUnitRunner` builds its fixture list as `suiteFixtureBefore :: suite.munitFixtures ::: suiteFixtureAfter`, so the suite's beforeAll/beforeEach run before the fixtures' and its afterEach/afterAll after them (runBeforeAll, runBeforeEach, runAfterEach, runAfterAll).

question: munit cross-builds for the JVM, Scala.js and Scala Native. How is its source tree split between shared and platform-specific code, what does each platform have to supply, and how do the Scala.js and Native builds run suites and report results without the real JUnit library?
reference: munit/shared holds the common API and `MUnitRunner`; the JVM build adds munit/jvm on top of the Java sbt/JUnit bridge in junit-interface (plus the real junit dependency); Scala.js and Native compile munit/js or munit/native together with munit/js-native, which supplies a minimal org.junit API (Description, RunNotifier, Filter) and the sbt test-interface `JUnitFramework`/`JUnitRunner`/`JUnitReporter`. Each platform has its own `PlatformCompat` (timeouts, awaiting, reflective suite instantiation) and its own `JUnitTask`, whose `MUnitRunNotifier` forwards the runner's notifications to `JUnitReporter`.

question: How are test failures modelled as exception types in munit, how do they relate to JUnit's failure types, and how does the runner react to each kind: an ordinary failed assertion, a request to abort the rest of the suite, an assumption that does not hold, and an error during per-test teardown?
reference: `FailExceptionLike` (munit/shared/src/main/scala/munit/FailExceptionLike.scala) is the common trait of `FailException` (an `AssertionError`) and `ComparisonFailException`, which extends JUnit's `ComparisonFailure` so IDEs can show a diff; `FailSuiteException` (a `FailException` thrown by `failSuite`) and the private `MUnitRunner.TestTeardownException` (wrapping afterEach errors) make `MUnitRunner.runTest` set `suiteAborted`, so later tests fail with 'Suite has been aborted'; JUnit's `AssumptionViolatedException` (from `assume`) is reported as an assumption failure, i.e. skipped.
